# Cluster Reference

This page is for setting up MicroCPipe on a new computer or cluster, and for
choosing how much memory and time to ask for. If you only want to run it on
a laptop, the default `profiles/local` needs no changes.

## How jobs are submitted

`sbatch MicroCPipe.sh` starts the launcher job (1 CPU, 16 GB, up to 10
days; it only schedules work). Inside it, Snakemake uses
`snakemake-executor-plugin-slurm` to submit each rule as its own SLURM job,
with the threads, memory and time set in the profile. SLURM job logs go to
`<outputDir>/logs_slurm`. The launcher also carries
`#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL,TIME_LIMIT_80`; add
`--mail-user=<your-email>` to the `sbatch` command to direct SLURM's own mail
(see [Running](running.qmd#email-notifications) for the workflow's emails).

## Profiles: one folder per site

Everything specific to a computer or cluster lives in one folder under
`profiles/`. The config and samplesheet are the same on every machine.

| Folder | For |
|--------|-----|
| `profiles/local/` | One machine with no scheduler (laptop, workstation, interactive node) |
| `profiles/biowulf/`, `profiles/longleaf/`, `profiles/pioneer/` | Examples of SLURM site profiles |
| `profiles/slurm-template/` | The starting point for any other SLURM cluster: copy it and fill in the `<...>` values |

::: {.callout-warning}
**Edit before use.** Account names, partitions, memory per node, time limits
and conda setup differ from site to site. The named profiles were written for
one site each, have not all been exercised end to end with MicroCPipe, and
contain account names that are not yours. Dry-run first, and watch the first
library on any new cluster.
:::

Each folder has two files:

- `env.sh`: sourced by `MicroCPipe.sh`, `MicroCMerge.sh` and `unlock.sh`;
  makes `python3` (>= 3.11) and `conda` (>= 24.7.1) available.
- `config.yaml`: the Snakemake profile: scheduler, account, partition, and
  each rule's threads, memory and time.

## Adding a new site

```bash
cp -r profiles/slurm-template profiles/mycluster
nano profiles/mycluster/config.yaml   # account, partition, limits
nano profiles/mycluster/env.sh        # how to get python3 + conda
echo 'export MICROC_PROFILE=profiles/mycluster' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
bash MicroCPipe.sh -n                  # dry run
sbatch MicroCPipe.sh
```

### Which keys to change in `config.yaml`

| Key | What to set |
|-----|-------------|
| `executor: slurm` | Leave as is for SLURM clusters |
| `jobs` | How many cluster jobs may be queued at once (default 100); lower it if your site limits submissions |
| `cores: 100` | Keep it. Without it Snakemake caps a rule's `threads` at the CPUs of the launcher job, so a rule that asks for 16 threads would run with 3 |
| `latency-wait` | Seconds to wait for output files to appear. Raise it on slow shared file systems |
| `default-resources: slurm_account` | Your SLURM account. Delete the line if your site has no accounts |
| `default-resources: slurm_partition` | A CPU partition you may use |
| `default-resources: runtime`, `mem_mb` | Defaults for any rule without its own entry. `runtime` is in **minutes**, `mem_mb` in **megabytes** |
| `set-threads:` | CPUs per rule (`align`, `dedup`, `split`, `sort_bam`, `hic` use 16; lower them if your nodes are small) |
| `set-resources:` | `runtime` (minutes) and `mem_mb` per rule; keep them below your partition's limits |

No GPU or QOS (quality-of-service) setting is needed by this pipeline. If your
site requires a QOS, add it under `default-resources` using the slurm executor
plugin's `slurm_extra` key (check the plugin documentation for the exact form).

### Finding your own values

```bash
sacctmgr show assoc user=$USER format=account%30,partition%20,qos%30   # your accounts
sinfo -s                                                             # partitions and their time limits
sinfo -o "%P %m %c"                                                  # partition, memory per node (MB), CPUs per node
```

Your site's documentation is the authority on node sizes, time limits and
which partition to use for CPU work. If you are unsure, ask your cluster's
support team.

### Writing `env.sh`

`env.sh` runs at the start of every launcher and has one job: make `python3`
(>= 3.11) and `conda` (>= 24.7.1) work. Pick whichever matches your site:

```bash
# A. Your own Miniforge (what the shipped files do; works almost everywhere)
source "${MICROC_CONDA_ROOT:-$HOME/miniforge3}/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"
conda activate base

# B. A module-based site
module load python/3.11 conda
source "$(conda info --base)/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"
conda activate base

# C. Inside an Apptainer / Singularity image that already holds python3 and conda
#    (run the launcher inside the container; env.sh can then be nearly empty)
```

Module names (`python/3.11` above) are only an example; use `module avail` to
see yours. Mamba works too if it provides the `conda` command.

## Choosing resources

### What each rule needs

The profile (not the rule) sets threads, memory and time. The shipped values
are conservative starting points. The table below is **one example, not a
benchmark and not an expected value**: 25 million read pairs, whole mouse
genome (mm10), one library, 16 threads where a rule uses them, on one SLURM
cluster (node types differ between clusters). Peak memory is `max_rss` from
Snakemake's benchmark files.

| Rule | Wall time | Peak memory |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| `align` (16 threads) | 28 min | about 23 GB |
| `dedup` | 8 min | not recorded here |
| `split` | 2 min | not recorded here |
| `sort_bam` | 0.5 min | not recorded here |
| `library_complexity` (preseq) | 3 min | not recorded here |
| `cool` | 0.5 min | not recorded here |
| `mcool` | 10 min | not recorded here |
| `hic` | 8 min | about 9 GB |

QC summary of that same run, to show what the dashboard numbers look like (one
example, not a target): 54% of read pairs mapped, 9% duplicates, 94% of
non-duplicate pairs cis, 56% cis >= 1 kb, 32% cis >= 10 kb.

**What this means.** For a library of this size the whole Core workflow takes
well under two hours of compute once the environments exist. Time and memory
grow with sequencing depth, so check your own `output/benchmarking.tsv` after
the first library and size the next, deeper one from it.

### Reading your own numbers

After any run, `output/benchmarking.tsv` (and the dashboard's Runtime &
memory table) lists, per group and rule, the run time (`s`, shown as h:mm:ss)
and peak memory (`max_rss`, in MB). Compare with what the profile requested:

- If a rule used far less than it asked for, lower `mem_mb` (on a busy cluster,
  smaller requests start sooner). The shipped `hic` request is much larger than
  the 9 GB seen in the example, to be safe for deeper libraries.
- If a rule came close to its request, raise it before the next, deeper
  library. As a rule of thumb (a suggestion, not a measured rule), request
  noticeably more than the peak you saw, since deeper libraries use more.

### Raising memory for `hic`, `dedup` and `align`

Edit `profiles/<site>/config.yaml` (memory in MB, time in minutes) and resubmit:

```yaml
set-resources:
  hic:
    mem_mb: 230000     # was 128000
    runtime: 1440
  dedup:
    mem_mb: 96000      # was 48000
  align:
    mem_mb: 48000      # was 32000
```

Check that the number is below the memory of your partition's nodes first
(`sinfo -o "%P %m"`).

`hic` is the rule most likely to need more memory for a deep library. It runs
`juicer_tools pre`, a Java program. Its Java heap follows the job's memory:
`javaMem` in `config/MicroCConfig.yaml` is empty by default, which means 85% of
`hic: mem_mb`, leaving room for Java's own overhead. If you set `javaMem`
yourself (for example `'96g'`), keep it below `hic: mem_mb`. If you cannot get
more memory, drop the finest entries of `hic_resolutions` (the `.mcool` keeps
them) or skip the `.hic` with `outputs: ['cool', 'mcool']`. A step-by-step
version is in [Recipes](recipes.qmd#when-the-hic-step-runs-out-of-memory).

After a memory or time failure: `bash unlock.sh` if a lock error appears, then
resubmit. Finished steps are kept.

### The local profile

`profiles/local/config.yaml` has no scheduler. It sets `cores: all` and a
global memory limit (`resources: mem_mb=64000`), and its per-rule `mem_mb`
values are accounting numbers Snakemake uses to avoid running too many heavy
jobs at once. Start it with `bash MicroCPipe.sh`. **Lower these numbers to fit
your machine**: the shipped `hic` request is 60000 MB, so a laptop with less
memory should lower both the global limit and `hic: mem_mb` (and, if you set it,
`javaMem`). A deep library may not fit on a workstation at all.

## Conda version {#conda-version}

Snakemake 8.27 needs conda >= 24.7.1 for its per-rule environments. Some
clusters' `conda` modules are older, so the shipped profiles use a Miniforge
install of your own (about 0.5 GB, one time):

```bash
wget https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh -b -p $HOME/miniforge3
```

`MICROC_CONDA_ROOT` points `env.sh` at it when it is not at
`$HOME/miniforge3`. Where the home directory is small, install it on a larger
file system (for example `/path/to/scratch/miniforge3`) and set
`MICROC_CONDA_ROOT`.

## Per-cluster settings

Two things differ between clusters. Both are set once per cluster and stay
out of git, so the same config and samplesheet run everywhere:

| Setting | How | Used by |
|---------|-----|---------|
| Compute profile | `export MICROC_PROFILE=profiles/<cluster>` in `~/.bashrc` | `MicroCPipe.sh`, `MicroCMerge.sh`, `unlock.sh` |
| Output location | `export MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT=/path/to/scratch/MicroCPipe` in `~/.bashrc` | every rule, and the SLURM log folder |

The profile is chosen by `--profile`, then `$MICROC_PROFILE`, then
`hpcProfile` in the config (default `profiles/local`). A relative `outputDir`
goes under `$MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT`, or under the launch folder if it is unset;
an absolute `outputDir` is used as written. On most sites SLURM jobs inherit
the environment of the shell that ran `sbatch`, so open a new shell (or
`source ~/.bashrc`) after editing it. A few sites are configured differently;
check yours.

## Site notes (examples)

These are examples of the kinds of difference you may meet, not instructions
for your cluster.

- **Accounts.** Some sites need `slurm_account` (the shipped `longleaf` and
  `pioneer` profiles contain an account name that is not yours; replace it); others have no
  accounts at all (the `biowulf` profile has none: delete the line).
- **Partitions and memory.** Nodes in a general partition may top out at a few
  hundred GB, and "big memory" partitions can have a minimum request. Check
  your site's limits before raising `hic: mem_mb`.
- **Small home directories.** Where home has a small quota, put the Miniforge
  install, caches and output on scratch (see
  [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd#moving-caches-to-scratch)).
- **Old conda modules.** Use your own Miniforge, as above.
- **Reference genomes.** Some sites provide pre-built BWA indexes; ask your
  support team where. Otherwise build one with `bwa index genome.fa`.

## Troubleshooting

See [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) for the full table. The ones that
come up when setting up a cluster:

| Symptom | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| `Error running conda info` | conda not on `PATH`: fix the conda line in `profiles/<site>/env.sh` |
| Invalid account or partition | `sacctmgr show assoc user=$USER`, `sinfo -s`; edit the profile |
| `hic` killed or Java heap error | Raise `hic: mem_mb` in the profile (above) |
| A rule ends in `TIMEOUT` | Raise that rule's `runtime:` (minutes), `bash unlock.sh`, resubmit |
| Output in the launch folder, not scratch | `MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT` not set in the shell that ran `sbatch` |
| Launcher `OUT_OF_MEMORY` on first run | Build the environments once on a compute node ([Setup](setup.qmd#conda-environments)) |
